Syllabus: Fundamentals of foreign exchange, Indian forex market, direct and indirect quotes, basic exchange-rate arithmetic, forward rates. Asked: 2–3 questions every session since Nov 2025. May 2026 asked:

  • exporter → buying rate
  • importer → selling rate
  • exporter and importer quoted forward rates from the same margins
  • a forward contract with a 3-month premium
  • a rupee amount for a USD purchase

1. Quotes

  • Direct quote: units of home currency per unit of foreign currency, e.g. USD/INR 83.25. India has used direct quotes since 2 August 1993.
    Indirect quote: foreign currency per unit of home currency, e.g. 1 INR = 0.01201 USD.
  • A two-way quote 83.25 / 83.33 is from the bank's side:
    • 83.25 = bid = the bank's buying rate
    • 83.33 = ask/offer = the bank's selling rate
    Buy low, sell high; the gap is the spread (the bank's margin).
  • Exporter or inward remittance: the customer sells USD to the bank → bank's buying rate (the lower one).
    Importer or outward remittance: the customer buys USD from the bank → bank's selling rate (the higher one).
  • Whether the deal is spot or forward does not change who is buying.

2. Merchant rates (FEDAI)

RateUsed forLevel
TT buyingClean inward remittances, export proceeds already credited to nostroHighest of the buying rates
Bill buyingPurchase or discount of export bills (bank pays before it receives)Lower than TT buying
TT sellingOutward remittances (not involving bills)Lowest of the selling rates
Bill sellingImport bills retired by the importerHigher than TT selling (extra handling)

Value dates: cash/ready = same day; TOM = next working day; spot = 2 working days (T+2); forward = beyond spot.

Nostro = our account with them (in foreign currency). Vostro = their account with us (in INR). Loro = their account with a third bank.

3. Forward rates

  • Forward rate = spot ± forward margin (swap points).
  • Margins in ascending order (e.g. 18/22) → foreign currency at a premium → add.
    Descending (e.g. 22/18) → discount → subtract.
  • Example: spot 83.42/83.48 with a 3-month margin of +18/+22 paise.
    • Forward buying (exporter) = 83.42 + 0.18 = 83.60.
    • Forward selling (importer) = 83.48 + 0.22 = 83.70.
    • The two customers are quoted different rates.
  • Annualised premium % = (Forward − Spot) ÷ Spot × (12 ÷ months) × 100. With spot 83.00 and a 3-month forward of 83.60 → 0.60 ÷ 83 × 4 × 100 = 2.89% p.a.
  • Interest rate parity: the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount.
    F = S × (1 + rINR × t) ÷ (1 + rUSD × t). With S = 83, rINR = 7%, rUSD = 5%, 3 months → F ≈ 83.41. The USD is at a premium because rupee rates are higher.

4. Cross rates

  • USD/INR 83.20/83.30 and GBP/USD 1.2600/1.2610:
    • GBP/INR bid = 83.20 × 1.2600 = 104.83
    • GBP/INR ask = 83.30 × 1.2610 = 105.04
  • Rule: for bid, multiply the bids; for ask, multiply the asks. When dividing, cross them.

5. Indian market basics

  • Governed by FEMA 1999. RBI regulates. FEDAI (Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India) sets the rules for interbank dealing.
  • Authorised Dealers:
    • Category I: banks
    • Category II: e.g. full-fledged money changers upgraded
    • Category III
  • Rupee is fully convertible on the current account, partially on the capital account.
  • FBIL publishes reference rates.
Traps:
  • "Selling rate whenever foreign currency is involved": wrong. Ask who is buying.
  • For the exporter use the lower rate (bank buys); for the importer the higher rate.
  • Ascending margin = premium (add). Descending = discount (subtract).
  • Spot settles T+2, not same day.
  • Bill buying rate < TT buying rate; bill selling rate > TT selling rate.

Syllabus: Capital structure, leverage, factors, theories (NI, NOI, traditional, MM), tax, cost of debt, preference and equity, WACC, factors affecting WACC, marginal cost of capital. Asked: 1–2 questions on WACC/cost each session, plus about 1 on theories. May 2026 asked:

  • financial leverage
  • "WACC is only a hurdle"
  • internal factors affecting WACC

Weighted marginal cost of capital, divisional cost of capital and floatation-cost detail are left out (not asked).

1. Cost of each source

SourceFormulaNote
Debt (irredeemable)Kd = I(1 − t) ÷ NPNP = net proceeds. Interest is tax-deductible, so debt is the cheapest source

2. CAPM and alpha

  • β measures systematic (market) risk, which can't be diversified away.
    • β > 1: aggressive
    • β < 1: defensive
    • β = 1: moves with the market
  • The security market line (SML) plots required return against β.
  • Alpha = actual (expected) return − CAPM required return. Positive alpha = the security lies above the SML (undervalued, outperforming) → buy.
  • Example: Rf 6%, Rm 14%.
    • A (β 0.8, 12%): required 12.4% → α −0.4
    • B (β 1.1, 16%): required 14.8% → α +1.2
    • C (β 1.6, 18%): required 18.8% → α −0.8
    Only B has positive alpha.

3. WACC

  • WACC = Σ (weight × after-tax cost).
  • Market-value weights are preferred; book-value weights are easier.
  • Example: equity 50% at 15%, preference 10% at 11%, debt 40% at 10% pre-tax, tax 25%.
    WACC = 7.5 + 1.1 + 0.4 × 7.5 = 11.6%.
  • WACC is the minimum hurdle rate for an average-risk project. A project much riskier than the firm needs a higher, risk-adjusted rate. "Accept every project above WACC" ignores project-specific risk.
  • Factors:
    • External (beyond the firm's control): level of interest rates, tax rates, market risk premium.
    • Internal (the firm's choice): capital-structure policy, dividend policy, investment policy.

4. Leverage

LeverageFormulaSource of risk
Operating (DOL)Contribution ÷ EBITFixed operating costs
Financial (DFL)EBIT ÷ EBT (= EBIT ÷ (EBIT − Interest))Fixed-cost funds (debt, preference)
Combined (DCL)DOL × DFL = Contribution ÷ EBTBoth
  • Example: contribution 80, EBIT 50, interest 10 → DOL 1.6, DFL 1.25, DCL 2.0. A 10% rise in sales lifts EPS by 20%.
  • Trading on equity: using debt raises EPS when the return on investment exceeds the cost of debt. It magnifies losses when it doesn't.

5. Capital structure theories

ApproachClaim
Net Income (NI) (Durand)More debt lowers WACC and raises firm value; Kd and Ke stay constant. So 100% debt is best.
Net Operating Income (NOI) (Durand)WACC and firm value are independent of capital structure. Ke rises with debt and offsets the cheaper debt.
TraditionalA moderate amount of debt lowers WACC up to a point, then risk raises it. An optimal capital structure exists.

With corporate tax: VL = VU + tD, because the interest tax shield raises value. Example: VU 100, debt 40, tax 30% → VL = 112.

Assumptions (NI/NOI/MM): no taxes (basic versions), no transaction costs, all earnings paid out, constant EBIT, perfect markets, and investors can borrow on the same terms as firms.

Factors in practice: cost, risk, control (debt avoids dilution), flexibility, tax, nature of business (stable cash flows can carry more debt), market conditions.

Traps:
  • Kd uses the after-tax rate. Preference dividend has no tax shield.
  • "Retained earnings have no cost": wrong. Their cost is the opportunity cost ≈ Ke.
  • Financial leverage comes from fixed-cost financing; operating leverage from fixed operating costs.
  • NI = debt helps; NOI = irrelevant; traditional = optimum exists.
  • Interest rates and tax rates are external factors affecting WACC.

Syllabus: Discounted and non-discounted cash-flow methods for investment appraisal, basic concepts of term loans, deferred payment guarantees, project finance, term-loan vs project appraisal. Asked: 2 questions every session on appraisal methods. May 2026 asked NPV/IRR concepts, the PV comparison inside lease-vs-buy, and a ₹45 crore plant decision.

1. Methods

MethodHowDecision ruleWeakness
Payback period (non-discounted)Time to recover the initial outlay from cash inflowsAccept if within the target periodIgnores time value and cash flows after payback
ARR (non-discounted)Average annual accounting profit ÷ average (or initial) investmentAccept if above the targetUses profit, not cash; ignores time value
Discounted paybackPayback using discounted inflowsAccept if within the targetStill ignores flows after payback
NPVPV of inflows − PV of outflows, at the cost of capitalAccept if NPV > 0Needs a discount rate. Best for mutually exclusive projects. Additive
IRRThe rate at which NPV = 0Accept if IRR > cost of capitalMultiple IRRs possible with non-conventional flows. Assumes reinvestment at the IRR

Same signal: NPV > 0 ⇔ IRR > k ⇔ PI > 1, for a single conventional project.

Conflict (mutually exclusive projects of different size or timing): follow NPV. NPV assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital, which is more realistic.

2. Worked example

Outlay ₹10 lakh; inflow ₹3 lakh a year for 5 years; k = 10% (PVAF 3.7908).

  • PV of inflows = 11.37 → NPV = +₹1.37 lakh; PI = 1.137.
  • Payback = 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33 years. Discounted payback ≈ 4.26 years.
  • IRR ≈ 15.24% (where PVAF = 10 ÷ 3 = 3.333).
  • ARR: depreciation 2 a year, so profit 1 a year. Average investment 10 ÷ 2 = 5 → ARR = 20%.

Uneven flows: outlay 5; inflows 1.5, 2, 2.5, 1 → payback = 2 years + 1.5 ÷ 2.5 = 2.6 years.

3. Cash flows to use

  • Use incremental, after-tax cash flows.
  • Add back depreciation (non-cash, but its tax shield counts).
  • Include: working capital invested (and recovered at the end), salvage value, and opportunity costs (e.g. the rent forgone on our own building).
  • Ignore sunk costs (a feasibility study already paid for).
  • Ignore financing costs (interest). They are captured in the discount rate.

4. Term loans and project finance (banker's view)

  • Term loan: more than 3 years (medium term 3–7, long term over 7) for fixed assets. Repaid from cash accruals, so the key test is DSCR (average 1.5–2).
    Other checks:
    • debt-equity (usually up to 2 : 1)
    • promoter's contribution
    • security cover
    • break-even
    • IRR
    • sensitivity
  • Project appraisal covers technical, economic or market, commercial, financial, managerial and environmental feasibility.
    Project finance (non-recourse or limited-recourse) relies on the project's own cash flows through an SPV, not the sponsor's balance sheet.
  • Term loan appraisal vs project appraisal: a term loan for an existing unit leans on its track record. A new project is appraised on projections and viability.
  • Deferred Payment Guarantee (DPG): the bank guarantees payment of instalments to a supplier of machinery who sells on deferred terms. It is a non-fund facility, but carries the same credit risk as a term loan.
Traps:
  • Payback and ARR ignore time value. ARR uses accounting profit.
  • For mutually exclusive projects, rank by NPV, not IRR or PI.
  • Do not deduct interest from project cash flows.
  • Sunk costs are ignored; opportunity costs are included.
  • Comparing undiscounted totals (e.g. total lease rentals vs price) is wrong.

Syllabus: Meaning, features and types of leases, rationale, lease agreement, legal aspects, finance vs operating lease, lease accounting, leasing as a financing decision. Asked: 1–2 questions on types and features per session since Nov 2025. May 2026 asked:

  • Ind AS 116 right-of-use asset
  • wet vs dry lease
  • lease-vs-buy by present value (three numericals)

Detailed lessor/lessee journal entries were asked only in 2024, so they are left out.

1. Parties and features

  • Lessor (owner) gives the lessee the right to use an asset for a period in return for lease rentals. Ownership stays with the lessor.
  • Leasing is governed by general law: the Indian Contract Act (bailment). There is no separate leasing Act. Stamp duty applies on the agreement.

2. Types

TypeMeaning
Finance leaseTransfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership.
  • Lease term covers most of the asset's life.
  • PV of rentals ≈ fair value.
  • Non-cancellable.
  • The lessee bears maintenance and insurance.
  • Often has a bargain purchase option.
  • "Full pay-out": the lessor recovers its whole investment plus return.
Operating leaseDoes not transfer substantially all risks and rewards.
  • Short-term and cancellable.
  • The lessor maintains the asset and bears obsolescence.
  • Rentals don't recover the full cost ("non-pay-out").
  • Examples: computers, aircraft hired for a season.
Sale and leasebackThe owner sells the asset to a lessor and leases it back. Releases cash while keeping use of the asset.
Direct leaseThe lessor buys from the supplier and leases to the lessee (two-party or three-party).
Leveraged leaseThree parties: lessor, lessee and lender. The lessor funds most of the cost by borrowing.
Cross-border leaseLessor and lessee are in different countries.
Wet leaseAircraft leased with crew, maintenance and insurance (ACMI) provided by the lessor. Short-term.
Dry leaseAircraft only. The lessee provides crew, maintenance and insurance. Usually longer-term, financing-type.

3. Accounting standards

  • AS 19 (non-Ind AS companies): the lessee capitalises a finance lease (asset + liability) and expenses operating-lease rentals. Land leases are excluded.
  • Ind AS 116 (lessee):
    • The finance/operating split is removed.
    • For almost every lease the lessee recognises a right-of-use (ROU) asset and a lease liability (PV of payments).
    • It depreciates the ROU asset and charges interest on the liability.
    • Exemptions: short-term leases (≤ 12 months) and low-value assets.
    • Legal ownership doesn't matter; control of an identified asset does.
  • Lessor under Ind AS 116 still classifies leases as finance or operating.
  • Lease vs hire purchase: in hire purchase, ownership passes to the hirer on paying the last instalment, and the hirer claims depreciation. In a lease, ownership stays with the lessor.

4. Lease vs buy (financing decision)

  • Compare the PV of lease rentals (after tax, discounted at the after-tax cost of borrowing) with the PV of the cost of buying: price − PV of the depreciation tax shield − PV of salvage.
  • The simple exam version: PV of rentals vs cash price.
    • ₹12 lakh × PVAF(10%, 5) 3.7908 = ₹45.49 lakh vs price ₹47.5 lakh → lease.
    • ₹10 lakh × PVAF(12%, 3) 2.4018 = ₹24.02 lakh vs price ₹24.5 lakh → lease.
    • ₹36 lakh × 3.7908 = ₹136.47 lakh vs price ₹152 lakh → lease.
  • If rentals are paid in advance, use annuity due: PVAF × (1 + r).

Rationale for leasing: 100% financing, preserves credit lines and working capital, tax benefits, protection from obsolescence (operating lease), quick and flexible.

Traps:
  • "Rent is an expense because ownership hasn't passed": wrong under Ind AS 116 (ROU asset + liability).
  • Wet = with crew; dry = aircraft only.
  • Operating lease: the lessor bears obsolescence. Finance lease: the lessee bears the risks.
  • Leveraged lease has a third party, the lender.
  • Compare PVs, never total rentals.

Syllabus: Working capital cycle, cash and marketable securities, accruals, trade credit, bank finance (methods, cash budget), regulation of bank finance, CP, factoring and forfaiting. Asked: 1 question on the WC cycle and 1 on sources every session. May 2026 asked: "when is WC requirement higher", internal sources of finance, liquidity ratios banks use, CP. Public deposits, ICDs and rights debentures are left out (not asked).

1. Concepts

  • Gross working capital = total current assets.
    Net working capital = CA − CL. It is the part of current assets financed by long-term funds (the margin).
  • Permanent (core) WC: the minimum always needed, so finance it long-term.
    Temporary (fluctuating) WC: seasonal, so finance it short-term.
  • Operating cycle = RM holding + WIP + FG holding + debtors' collection period − creditors' payment period (net cycle).
    A longer cycle means a higher WC requirement.
  • WC need is higher when:
    • production is long (heavy engineering)
    • the business is seasonal
    • generous credit is given to buyers and little received from suppliers
    • growth is rapid
    • inflation is high
    It is lower for cash businesses and service firms (restaurants, utilities).
  • Sources:
    • Internal: retained earnings, depreciation provision, accruals (outstanding wages and taxes).
    • External: trade credit, bank finance, CP, factoring, ICDs, public deposits.

2. Bank finance for working capital

MethodContent
Tandon Committee (1975) — MPBFWorking-capital gap (WCG) = CA − CL other than bank borrowings.
  • Method I: MPBF = 75% of WCG (borrower brings 25% of WCG).
  • Method II: MPBF = 75% of CA − other CL (borrower brings 25% of CA), so the minimum current ratio is 1.33 : 1.
  • Method III: like II but excluding core current assets, which the borrower finances fully.
Nayak Committee — turnover methodFor small borrowers (MSEs with limits up to ₹5 crore): WC need = 25% of projected annual turnover. Bank finances 20%; the borrower's margin is 5% of turnover.
Cash budget methodFor seasonal industries (sugar, tea) and large borrowers: limits fixed from monthly cash-flow deficits.
Loan system for delivery of bank creditRBI 2018: for borrowers with aggregate fund-based WC limits of ₹150 crore and above, at least 40% must be a WC loan (from 1 Oct 2018), raised to 60% from 1 April 2019. The rest can be cash credit. This forces credit discipline.

Drawing power = (stock + eligible receivables) − margin, capped by the sanctioned limit. Banks monitor it through stock statements and stock audits.

3. Commercial Paper (CP)

  • A short-term unsecured money-market instrument issued as a promissory note at a discount, in demat form.
  • Tenor: 7 days to 1 year.
  • Denomination: ₹5 lakh and multiples.
  • Issuers: companies, NBFCs (including HFCs), all-India financial institutions and other eligible body corporates. Credit rating required.
  • Banks do not issue CP; they raise short-term funds through Certificates of Deposit (CD).
  • Regulated by RBI. CP is cheaper than bank credit for highly rated firms.

4. Factoring vs forfaiting

FactoringForfaiting
ReceivablesOngoing, short-term (up to 180 days), domestic and export, open accountOne-off export receivables, medium-term (often 1–5 years), backed by bills / LC / aval
RecourseWith or without recourseWithout recourse
FinanceAdvance of 75–90%100% of the value (discounted)
ServicesAlso sales-ledger management and collectionPure financing
LawFactoring Regulation Act 2011—

TReDS: an electronic platform where MSME invoices on large buyers are financed by multiple financiers, without recourse to the MSME.

Traps:
  • A longer operating cycle means more working capital. A longer creditors' period means less.
  • Tandon Method II → minimum current ratio 1.33.
  • Nayak: 25% of turnover, of which 20% is bank finance and 5% margin.
  • CP is unsecured, at a discount, and not for banks.
  • Forfaiting is without recourse, 100% finance, export-only.
C10:
Syllabus: Derivatives: characteristics and functions, users, futures, FRA, swaps, options. Asked: about 1 question on types per session. May 2026 asked about exchange-traded derivatives (ETDs) and a statement on derivatives and forward contracts in India. The theory of characteristics and functions (asked only in 2024) is kept to a few lines.

1. Meaning and users

  • A derivative is a contract whose value comes from an underlying: a currency, interest rate, share, index or commodity.
  • Users:
    • Hedgers reduce risk.
    • Speculators take risk for profit.
    • Arbitrageurs profit from price differences between markets, without risk.
  • Regulation in India:
    • Exchange-traded derivatives (equity, currency and interest-rate futures and options on NSE/BSE): SEBI.
    • OTC interest-rate and forex derivatives (forwards, swaps, FRAs): RBI.
    • Commodity derivatives: SEBI (since the FMC merger in 2015).

2. Types

InstrumentFeatures
ForwardOTC, customised (amount and date). Settled at maturity. Counterparty (default) risk. No margin, not marked to market. Both parties are obliged.
FuturesExchange-traded, standardised (lot size, expiry). The clearing corporation is the counterparty, so there is no counterparty risk. Initial margin + daily mark-to-market. Highly liquid and can be squared off anytime.
OptionsThe buyer (holder) pays a premium and gets a right but not an obligation. The seller (writer) has the obligation.
  • Call = right to buy. Put = right to sell.
  • American = exercise any time up to expiry. European = only on expiry.
  • Call is in the money when spot > strike; put when spot < strike.
  • The buyer's maximum loss = premium. The writer's loss can be unlimited (for a call).
SwapsExchange of cash flows.
  • Interest rate swap: fixed vs floating in one currency. Notional principal is not exchanged.
  • Currency swap: principal and interest in two currencies. Principal is exchanged at the start and the end.
FRA (Forward Rate Agreement)OTC contract fixing an interest rate today for a future period on a notional amount. Only the difference is settled (discounted, at the start of the period). Quoted as "3×6": starts in 3 months, ends in 6. A buyer of an FRA is protected against rising rates.
Credit default swapProtection buyer pays a premium; the seller pays if the reference entity defaults.

3. ETD vs OTC

Exchange-tradedOTC
Standardised contractsCustomised
Clearing corporation guarantees (novation)Counterparty credit risk
Margins and daily MTMUsually no daily margin (collateral may be agreed)
Transparent prices, liquidLess transparent; reported to the trade repository (CCIL)
e.g. currency futures and options, index futurese.g. forex forwards, IRS, FRA, currency swaps
Traps:
  • A forward obliges both sides. An option obliges only the writer.
  • Futures carry no counterparty risk because the clearing house guarantees them. Forwards do.
  • IRS: notional is never exchanged. Currency swap: principal is exchanged.
  • FRA settles only the interest difference, not the principal.
  • American options can be exercised early; European only at expiry.
